title: Bina and tevuna: the recap of chapters one and two, and seeing G-d in the shtender
overview:
Rabbi Markel calls chapter three "really a recap chapter": the conclusion of chapters one and two, applied to contemplating G-dliness, with *memalei kol almin*, the coming into being of something from nothing, as the example. Contemplation has two levels. *Bina* is the grasp of the concept itself: its *orech* brings it down into *meshalim*, a physical garment a child could grasp; its *rochav* explains it in many ways; and only after both comes the depth, which looks like the *kitzur* and is not. *Daas* binds the mind to what it understood and brings it to the depth of *chachma* (wisdom), where the mind sees the truth instead of following an explanation.

*Tevuna* brings that depth down into what the eyes see. The Alter Rebbe *davened* "with the *shtender*": he saw that the *shtender* is *Elokus* (G-dliness), as one sees the hidden bunnies once they are pointed out. Without *tevuna* Chassidus stays an abstract puzzle ("What's it good for?"), contemplation in prayer becomes spacing out, and G-d and the world stay two things. The real *tevuna* is *ein od milvado*: you want the health and the money for the Chassidus.

sections.title: Two levels of contemplation; bina is the grasp of the concept itself, down to its depth
sections.summary: The chapter sums up chapters one and two: contemplating G-dliness has two levels, *bina* and *tevuna*. *Bina* is the grasp of the concept itself, in all its details, as with *memalei kol almin*, studied from its outside to its inside until one reaches the *omek hamusag*.

phrases.he: (ג) ובכל זה יובן בענין ההתבוננות
בהשגת האלקות,
שיש ב' מדריגות, בינה ותבונה.
בינה היינו בחינת עצם ההשגה האלקית בכל פרט
ענין שמתבונן,
איך הוא
ומה הוא,
ועומד על הדבר בעיון רב בכל פרטי חלקיו
כו' כנזכר לעיל

blocks.text: Chapter three is basically the conclusion of chapters one and two. With all this the *hisbonenus* in grasping G-dliness will be understood: it has two levels, *bina* and *tevuna*. *Bina* is the grasp itself, in every detail, how it is and what it is, gone over with much *iyun*: in other words, the actual learning.

phrases.he: כמו בהשגה פרטיות דממלא כל עלמין
שהוא התהוות יש מאין
הנקרא כח הפועל האלקי בנפעל כו'
והוא בחינת שם אדנ״י או שם אלהי״ם,
לשון כח כידוע.
הנה יש בזה כמה חלוקי פרטים
באופני חיצוניות הענין
עד אשר יושג תוך תוך הענין הזה
בפנימית העצמי, איך שהוא בעצם כו'
שזהו הנקרא עומק המושג כו'
כנזכר לעיל שהעיון הוא בחינת כלי
לבא לבחינת העומק כו'

blocks.text: The example is the grasp of *memalei kol almin*, the coming into being of something from nothing, called the *koach hapoel banifal*. This is the Name *Adnus* or the Name *Elokim*, both words that mean power.

blocks.question: Is it the Name Adam here, or *Adnus*?
blocks.text: The old copy reads the Name Adam (and Adam is *MaH*); another has *alef-dalet*, *Adnus*; someone suggests the Name of G-d. The reading *Adnus* actually makes more sense.

The outside of *memalei kol almin* has many distinctions of detail, until its very inside is grasped, how it is in its essence: this is the *omek hamusag*. The *iyun* is a *kli* to come to that depth, and later on to how the inner [light] works in the *seder hishtalshelus* (the chain of worlds).

sections.title: Length and breadth: one concept brought close in meshalim and explained in many ways
sections.summary: The *orech* (length) brings the concept down into *meshalim*, a physical garment, until a child could grasp it. The *rochav* (breadth) explains it in many different ways, through spreading forth from the essence and through revealing the hidden, each with many *meshalim* of its own; the opposite of both is the *kitzur*.

phrases.he: ובחינת האורך הוא בחינת התקרבות הענין הזה אל השכל
במשלים שונים הידועים
עד שיהיה הדבר הזה קרוב במוחו מאד
(בל"א אראפ גילאזן זייער דעם שכל צו זיך)
phrases.en: He brings the *sechel* very close to himself.

phrases.he: בלבוש הגשמה,
עד שיוכל תינוק להשיג כו' כנזכר לעיל

blocks.text: The *orech* (length) brings this matter close to the *sechel* (intellect) through the various known *meshalim* (analogies). He does not stop to explain it: the author is recapping what he has already said, and it is pretty much self-explanatory.
Until it is very close in his mind; the Yiddish says: he brings the *sechel* very close to himself. The *meshalim* are a physical garment, until a child could grasp it.

phrases.he: והרוחב היינו להרחיב זה הדבר כמו שהוא בכמה אופנים שונים,
ולא באופן א' לבד
כמו המשל לזה הדבר מחיי הנפש בגוף,
שאין זה רק התפשטות מן העצם כידוע
phrases.en: The *chayus hanefesh baguf* is *hispashtus min ha'etzem*.

blocks.text: The *rochav* (breadth) broadens the same thing in many different ways, not in one alone: for instance the *mashal* of the life of the soul in the body, which is a *hispashtus min ha'etzem*.

phrases.he: ויש רבוי אופנים למאוד בהתפשטות מן העצם
phrases.en: There's various *meshalim* in *hispashtus min ha'etzem*.

phrases.he: וגם בגלוי ההעלם,
כתנועת החי וכאותיות הדבור כו'
או כהתחכמות מן עצם החכמה
או כגלוי הראיה דעין
או כגלוי שלהבת מן הגחלת כו'
וכל זה נקרא גלוי ההעלם

blocks.text: There are very many *meshalim* for spreading forth from the essence, and also for *gilui ha'helem*. So *memalei kol almin* is explained in a few ways: one is spreading forth from the essence, which itself has a bunch of *meshalim*; another is revealing the hidden.

Revealing the hidden too comes in various ways: the movement of a living creature, the letters of speech, reasoning out of the essence of *chachma*, the sight of the eye, a flame from the coal. Each is a different way of saying it. All of it is "the *rochav* of one *orech*", the *orech* of revealing the hidden.

phrases.he: מה שאין כן משל זיו השמש
או אור הנר וכח הפועל כו'
שנקרא התפשטות כו' וכהאי גוונא
הרי כל זה בעצם הענין
phrases.en: But all of this is still about the *etzem ha'inyan* of *memalei kol almin*;

phrases.he: רק שנתרחב,
phrases.en: he widens it out.

phrases.he: וההיפך מזה הוא הקיצור
רק באופן אחד,
phrases.en: narrow,

phrases.he: וגם הוא בדרך קצרה
phrases.en: and also that in a short way of length,

phrases.he: נסקר במוחו בלתי התפשטות להרחיב בו כלל כו'

blocks.text: Whereas the sun's radiance, a candle's light and the power of the maker are called spreading forth from the essence: a different *orech*, which also has various ways to explain it.

All of this is still the essence of *memalei kol almin*, only widened out. Its opposite is the *kitzur* (shortening), short in both width and length: in one way only, which is narrow, and briefly. The thing is glanced over in the mind, without broadening it at all.

sections.title: The depth comes only after length and breadth, in every concept of G-dliness
sections.summary: The depth reached after all the *meshalim* and explanations looks like the *kitzur* and is not. Everything chapter one said of *Keser* (crown), *chachma* and *bina* of *bina* is found in a particular concept like *memalei kol almin*, and in every particular of G-dliness the book will explain.

phrases.he: אבל כמו שזה הדבר נתפס לעומקו בעצם,
אחר כל רבוי הסבר דמיון המשלים,
הוא הנקרא עומק ותמצית זה המושג כנזכר לעיל
ודווקא אחר האריכות והרוחב במשלים בעיון רב
יבא לבחינת העומק שמובן מהם,
(בל"א דער הערין דיא טיפקייט פון דעם וויא דיא זאך איז באמת)
phrases.en: (to understand the real deepness of this thing, how the thing really is),

phrases.he: דהיינו אחר הלבשת חיצוניותו בכל העיון הרב כו'
ודי למבין

blocks.text: That was the *kitzur*. But the thing grasped to its depth, in essence, after all the explanations and *meshalim*, is called the depth and essence of the concept. It looks the same as the *kitzur*, but it really is not.

*Davka* after the length and breadth of *meshalim*, with much *iyun*, one comes to the depth understood from them, as in what was said about the Alter Rebbe, or the Deitschel and the dead man. The Yiddish: to perceive **the real deepness of this thing, how the thing really is**. With this passage he has recapped chapter one.

phrases.he: (וכל מה שכתבנו למעלה בכל פרטי כח''ב דבינה,
phrases.en: (And the whole thing was explained above in chapter one in *Keser*, *chachma* and *bina* of *bina*:

phrases.he: הכל ימצא בהשגה פרטיות כזאת,
phrases.en: in any *hasaga pratis* throughout the book, you'll find this whole *inyan* of the *havana* of the *bina* of the thing.

phrases.he: וכהאי גוונא
phrases.en: The same like you'll find it in the *inyan* of *memalei kol almin*,

phrases.he: בכל השגת אלקות הפרטים9 וכמשי"ת)
phrases.en: in any *hasaga* of *Elokus*, the *pratim* of it, and how it's going to be explained later in the book.)

blocks.text: Up to now he has explained *bina* and applied it to *memalei kol almin*: going through it with all the details, all the different *meshalim* and explanations, whether spreading forth or revealing. That is the breadth. The length brings each one down into *meshalim*, into physical terms: revealing the hidden is like the letters of speech revealing the letters of thought, or like the *mashal* of a river.

All of chapter one's *Keser*, *chachma* and *bina* of *bina* is here: the *bina* of *bina* is the *hisbonenus*; the *chachma* of *bina* is discovering a new thing within the same thing; the *Keser* is the *omek hamusag*; and deeper still, the *Keser* of the *shaar hanun* (the fiftieth gate).
All of it is found in any particular grasp throughout the book: as in *memalei kol almin*, so in every particular of G-dliness that will be explained later. So he has recapped what *bina* is.

sections.title: Daas: the bond with the concept, and the depth of chachma, where the mind sees
sections.summary: *Daas* is recognising and feeling what one has understood, bound to it; the mitzva to know G-d is *davka* in *memalei kol almin*. It brings to the depth of *chachma*, the *re'iyas hasechel*, where one no longer follows an explanation but sees the truth of it.

phrases.he: ובחי' הדעת הוא בחינת ההכרה והרגשה במושכל
בהתקשרות
כנזכר לעיל
phrases.en: like he explained before.

phrases.he: ועל זה נאמר וידעת כו'
דע את אלה״י כו'
שהוא בהשגה זו דממלא כל עלמין דוקא כידוע
phrases.en: This *inyan* of the mitzva of *daas Havaya* is *davka* in the *inyan* of *memalei kol almin*.

blocks.text: *Daas* is recognising and feeling the *muskal* (the thing understood), bound to it. Of it is said "And you shall know" and "Know the G-d of your father": the mitzva of *daas Havaya* (knowing G-d) is *davka* in *memalei kol almin*. That is one meaning of "the earth shall be full of knowledge of G-d as the waters cover the sea."

*Daas Havaya*, then, is *davka* in the *seder hishtalshelus*. Rabbi Markel thinks that, looked at closer, it is really *davka* in *Beriya*, *Yetzira* and *Asiya*, more than higher up; though *Havaya* is basically the four worlds, *Atzilus*, *Beriya*, *Yetzira* and *Asiya*.
So *daas* is *davka* in the grasp: having *daas* enter it and be bound to it, *davka* the *daas Havaya* of *memalei kol almin*. The Yiddish calls it *der klepp*.

phrases.he: (בל"א דער קלעפ כו' כנ"ל באורך)
phrases.en: (*Klepp* is the holding onto the *davka* in the length of the thing),

phrases.he: שהוא דוקא המביא לבחינת עומקא דכולא,
phrases.en: *davka* the *hisbonenus* is *davka* what brings to the *omka d'chula*,

phrases.he: דהיינו לעומק דחכמה שמאין תמצא כנזכר לעיל
phrases.en: the *taalumos chachma*, like he explained before,

phrases.he: דהיינו בבחינת עומק ראיות השכל
phrases.en: when you see the thing with your mind,

phrases.he: בהשגה זו דבחינת מלא כל עלמין
שלמעלה מהשגת השכל כידוע

blocks.text: *Klepp*, he thinks, is the holding on, *davka* in the length of the thing. It is *davka* the *hisbonenus* that brings to the *omka d'chula*, the depth of everything: the depth of *chachma*, the *taalumos chachma* (the hidden depths of wisdom) that come after the *hisbonenus*, "which is found from nothing."

That is the depth of *re'iyas hasechel*, seeing with the mind. It is not the seeing of prophecy, which is *mamash* with the eyes. *Re'iyas hasechel* means something is explained well enough that you see the truth of it: it is no longer an explanation; you *mamash* see the truth of it.

blocks.question: Doesn't the Rebbe say that even physical seeing comes out of *hisbonenus*?
blocks.text: Physical sight does come out of *hisbonenus*; everything does. But here it is *re'iyas hasechel*. The student presses: when the Rebbe in the *sicha* (talk) speaks of pointing with the finger and saying "this", that is *davka* physical sight. Exactly: that is the eyes, and here he is talking of *re'iyas hasechel*, called the seeing of *chachma*.

phrases.he: (וכמו שכתוב ברעיא מהימנא,
בעין בשכל, דבלבא אתחזי כולא,
phrases.en: With the eye of the *sechel* within the heart, everything is seen,

phrases.he: ונקרא לאסתכלא ביקרא כו'
phrases.en: and this is called to see the *kavod* of the King.

phrases.he: וגם בזה יש בחינת עומק כנזכר לעיל באריכות)
phrases.en: This also has an *omek*, like we explained before.)

blocks.text: As the *Ra'aya Mehemna* says: with the eye of the *sechel* within the heart, everything is seen; and this is called gazing at the glory of the King. This too has depth: in *chachma* too there is a length, a breadth and a depth. That is chapter one, up to here.

sections.title: Tevuna: bringing the hidden depth down until you see G-d in the world
sections.summary: *Tevuna* draws the hidden depth of the concept down into revelation, all the way into what the eyes see, so that one sees the world itself as G-dliness, like the hidden bunnies in a picture once someone points them out. One who has absorbed the concept can bring it into the details of how each created thing comes into being.

phrases.he: ובחינת התבונה
היינו לדלות על ידו מעומק זה הנעלם
במושג זה דממלא כל עלמין הנזכר לעיל
לידי גילוי,
phrases.en: into a revelation.

phrases.he: כי בהיותו קולט בכי טוב לעצם ההשגה הזאת,
על כן יוכל להביאה בכמה ענינים נבדלים ממנה

blocks.text: Now to chapter two: *tevuna*. Remember, the whole exile is *davka* because of the lack of *tevuna*. *Bina* is missing too ("My people does not contemplate"), but even more *tevuna*.

*Tevuna* draws up from this hidden depth: not the depth of *bina* but of *chachma*, where you *mamash* see the verity of the explanation. Not that you see the explanation: through it you see how it actually is, in a mental way. *Tevuna* brings it into revelation.

And this, by the way, is where actual seeing with the eye comes in: bringing it down so that you *mamash* see the G-dliness in the physical world, in what is actually happening, so that when you see the physical world... (a phone call cuts him off).
He reads it again: *tevuna* draws it up into revelation. And as he said, the real seeing with the eyes is like that.

blocks.title: "With the shtender"
blocks.text:
*Tevuna* means the understanding is no longer abstract: you bring it all the way down into what you are seeing.

The Alter Rebbe asked the Mitteler Rebbe what he had *davened* with: with a *hisbonenus* about *Adam Kadmon*. And what had the Alter Rebbe *davened* with? "With the *shtender*."

What does that mean? That he held on to it, as a joke? No: he saw that the *shtender* itself is *Elokus*. That is *tevuna*: you look around, apply the whole *bina*, and realise you are looking at nothing but G-d, *ein od milvado* (there is nothing besides Him). You are actually looking at G-d right now, and you were the whole time; the thing is knowing how to parse it.

blocks.title: Find the ten bunnies
blocks.text: So do you see G-d more than somebody else? He sees the same physical world you do. It is like the puzzles in the kiddie magazines where you have to find the ten bunnies hidden in a picture. The leaves of a tree look like leaves, and then, looking closely, there is an upside-down bunny.

blocks.title: Once you see the bunny
blocks.text: Looking at the picture, you are seeing the ten bunnies, just not aware of them: you see them the same before you find them as after. Once you have found them you can point: there it is. And once you found the bunny, "it's hard to make it look like leaves again", as with optical illusions: once you see it properly, it is hard not to.

"You are a G-d who hides." But once you see it, or somebody shows you (here is his nose, there are his feet), you see it. That is what the Rebbe [the author] is going to show us in this book: where the ten bunnies are.

Before, you saw everything there is to see in the picture; you just did not notice the bunny. After somebody shows you, you are not seeing more: exactly the same picture, "and yet, now you see the bunnies with your physical eyes." So with an explanation: it tells you there are ten bunnies in the picture in front of your eyes, and you ask where they are.

Now you see: here is His hand, *chesed* the right arm; here is the other, *gevura* the left; here is the hand of G-d. So the magicians in Egypt saw the finger of G-d, and later the hand of G-d: "They didn't see any hand, but they saw a thing that was the hand of G-d."

For he takes in the essence of this grasp thoroughly: understanding what he is going to explain is not enough; one has to go over it a few more times until it is absorbed. Then he can bring it into matters separate from it.

phrases.he: כמו בכמה פרטי מציאות עולמות הנבראים,
איך שמתהווים מאין ליש
בבחינת ממלא דרך פרט
אשר נעלם בכללות השגה זו כו'
phrases.en: This is hidden, like the bunnies, in the general *hasaga* that he had before.

blocks.text: Such as the details of the created worlds, how each comes into being from nothing to something through *memalei* in a particular way, which is hidden in the general grasp: **hidden, like the bunnies**.

sections.title: Without tevuna Chassidus is a puzzle on the side: "What's it good for?"
sections.summary: Without *tevuna* the concept stays in the mind and a person does not know what to do with it, even though he understood it well; he thinks contemplation in prayer means spacing out on abstract things, when prayer is bringing G-d down into the world. For him G-d and the world are two things; the real *tevuna* is *ein od milvado*, where what one really wants is the Chassidus itself.

phrases.he: ובלתי כח התבונה הזאת בהשגה זו שממלא כל עלמין
הרי נשארת השגה זו רק במוח הבנתו לבד,
ולא ידע מה לעשות בה
phrases.en: And he doesn't know what to do with it,

phrases.he: ואיך להביא זאת ההתבוננות באיכות ענין התהוות היש מאין כלל,
phrases.en: and how to bring this whole *hisbonenus* into an actual *havana* of how the actual world comes something from nothing,

phrases.he: כמובן מכל הנזכר לעיל ודי למבין

blocks.text: Without this *tevuna*, there are a whole lot of people all over the place studying Chassidus who have no *tevuna* in it. Why? The grasp stays in the mind alone, and **he doesn't know what to do with it**.

People ask what learning *Ayin Beis* is good for. Will it make money? Improve *middos*? A *mussar* book will do that; this is just an intellectual thing, "good for people who like to do mathematical acrostic puzzles." Or: how does it help with the *davenen*?
Nor does he know how to bring this *hisbonenus* into an actual understanding of how the world comes to be something from nothing, instead of a bunch of abstract explanations.

phrases.he: (ומזה מובן סיבת המניעה בחדשים או גם בישנים
בחסרי תבונה,
גם שמשיגים היטב הדק בשעה ששומעים ורואים,
phrases.en: They learn *Chassidus* actually, and they understood it;

phrases.he: לא יוכלו להביא הדבר כלל בהתבוננות בתפלה בענין התהוות העולמות
phrases.en: they cannot bring it in the *hisbonenus* of the *tefilla*,

blocks.text: This explains what holds back the new ones, and the old ones too: they lack *tevuna*. They learned Chassidus, the *sichos* (talks), and understood it, maybe not every last detail; yet they cannot bring it into *hisbonenus* in *tefilla*: not necessarily in *tefilla*, but in an actual relationship to the world.
By the way, when people think of *hisbonenus* in *tefilla*, they think it means thinking about abstract things during the *tefilla*: sitting there in the *tefilla* and spacing out.

But the height of the whole *tefilla* is asking the *Aibershter* (the One Above) to make you healthy, give you money, bring us back to Jerusalem, build the Temple. *Tefilla* is asking Him to connect: "Blessed are You" means bring Yourself down to here; *baruch* means to bring down, like *bereicha* (a pool).

Bring Yourself down to here: revive the dead; forgive us, our Father, for we have sinned; give us a livelihood, give us health; bring us back to Jerusalem, rebuild the Temple and its service, "and we can all sit and learn Chassidus the whole time."

Lacking *tevuna*, they think *hisbonenus* in *tefilla* is spacing out on abstract things, when really *tefilla* means bringing G-dliness down into the world, in actual physical things. *Tefilla* is asking the *Aibershter* to take over the world, to bring Moshiach; there is a prayer for that.
They do not see what the *hisbonenus* of how *Atik* and *Arich* (levels of *Keser*) are two sides of the same thing has to do with getting money, or with anything at all.

This is about *avodas halev* (the service of the heart) and *tefilla*, even *avodas hamochin*, and certainly *daas Havaya*, which will be the real thing of Moshiach. Not only in *tefilla*: in everything you do, you are to see that it is no accident; it is literally the *Aibershter* doing it all. Belief in *hashgacha pratis* (divine providence) is one thing; you are supposed to actually see it. So even though they understand it fine, they have no understanding [of what to do with it].

phrases.en: (Nothing but the idea itself is what he has.)

phrases.he: וד"ל16:

blocks.text: Until he asks what he is going to do with all this Chassidus, and what use he needs it for.

There is an even higher thing: not that Chassidus is for the money, but that when you ask for a livelihood, Chassidus is the livelihood. What he wants is *davka* the Chassidus itself, not the Chassidus as a means to other things; if anything, the money is for the Chassidus.

For in his mind they are two separate things: Chassidus and the world have nothing to do with each other. The world is the world, and on Shabbos you sit with your friends and "play a crossword puzzle of Chassidus a little bit, and that's it." Only the understanding itself stays in his mind, separate from everything.

In Yiddish: the *muskal* alone, by itself. **Nothing but the idea itself is what he has**, connected to nothing: abstract thoughts with absolutely no relationship to the world, to his life. And this is enough for one who understands.

There are levels to "two separate things". In one it is totally abstract, with nothing to do even with what one asks in *tefilla*. In the other it brings the light down so you get things in the world, but it is still two things: G-d, and the world, and you asking G-d to help you. That is already some *tevuna*, that something will come of it.

That is not the real *tevuna*. The real *tevuna* is *ein od milvado*: what you really want is the Chassidus. You do not want the Chassidus to help you with the health; it is the opposite: you want the health and the money for the Chassidus. "If we were all healthy and we had a whole bunch of money, we could all sit together and learn Chassidus all the time." And it is all one thing.

This was really a recap chapter.

reviewQuestions.question: What are the *orech* and the *rochav* of *bina*, and what is the *kitzur* that is the opposite of both?
Why are the movement of a creature, the letters of speech and the flame from the coal the *rochav* of one *orech*?
If the depth reached after length and breadth looks like the *kitzur*, how is it different?
How is the *re'iyas hasechel* different from the seeing of prophecy, and from pointing with a finger and saying "this"?
What did the Alter Rebbe mean when he said he *davened* "with the *shtender*", and what do the ten bunnies add?
Why do people who understand Chassidus well still ask "What's it good for?", and what is the real *tevuna* about health, money and Chassidus?

notes.text: Line 4: he reads "shem Adam" (and remarks "Adam is MaH"); a student's book has alef-dalet (Ad-nai). He has "the old one" and says the other reading "makes more sense". Who holds which book is not certain from the transcript; the phrases follow the printed text (Adnus).

Line 5: the half-sentence after "the iyun is a kli" (021 w212-233) is broken ("the iyun into, in other words, later on the whole inyan of how the pnimi works in the seder hishtalshelus"); the block renders it as "to come later on to how the inner [light] works in the seder hishtalshelus". Check against the audio.

Line 15: "like the thing we said about the Alter Rebbe or the Deitschel and the mes" (021 w656-671) points back to a story told in an earlier class (probably one of the chapter 10-15 classes recorded first); it is not told here, and the block keeps only the reference.

Line 22: the sentence ending at 021 w1712 ("so that when you see the physical world, Hello, Shimon?") is cut off by the phone call; the block leaves it unfinished. The story of the shtender is introduced at the end of the sentence w1777-1836, so the story's audio starts at w1777 with his tevuna lead-in.
Line 19: he reads "der klepp" tentatively ("I think klepp is the holding onto..."); reported as his reading.

Lines 19-20: "the Rebbe" in the student's question (021 w1325-1418), with the talk about pointing with a finger, is presumably the Lubavitcher Rebbe; at w2367 "what the Rebbe is going to show us in this book" is the author, marked [the author].

Line 22: he says the magicians saw the finger of G-d "when the Jews went up out of Egypt" and "later on they saw the hand of G-d". In the verses the magicians say "the finger of G-d" at the plague of lice (Exodus 8:15), and Israel sees "the great hand" at the sea (Exodus 14:31). The block keeps what he said.

Line 22: the alignment mark (conf 0.42) is at w1740, but he starts tevuna at w1513 ("Now he's getting to chapter two"); all of w1513-2702 is under this line. His rereading at w2650 is garbled ("ki b'yeser kelipas hachitzonim"); the phrase "for since he takes in the essence of this grasp thoroughly" follows the printed text and his explanation ("go over it a few more times till you absorb it").

Lines 6, 7, 25-26: he reads some words differently from the printed text (line 6 "hesbaras" (explaining) for "hiskarvus" (bringing close); line 7 the Yiddish "er hot gebracht" (he brought) for "arop gelozn" (lowered, let down), which the phrase marks as [lit. lowers]; "hachiluk" for "hadak", "ad shetishaer" for "ad sheyishal", "shenishar rak bechinas avoda atzma umocho nivdal"); the phrases follow the printed text. He translates hardly any of lines 1-21 phrase by phrase ("I'm not translating or explaining because... he's recapping"); there the phrases are a plain rendering in the words of his explanation.

No block is flagged for sensitivity: the class has no remark about women, other religions, politics or a named person. The sharpest remarks (people "all over the place studying Chassidus" with no tevuna, sitting in prayer and spacing out, the Shabbos "crossword puzzle of Chassidus") are criticism of an attitude, not of a group, and are kept as he said them.
